--- title: "Missing values, outliers and imbalance" description: "What to do about the damage once you have found it — and why the right answer is a scientific judgement rather than a default." order: 4 categories: [data-preparation, class-imbalance, marine-data] --- ## Why this matters Every fix in this page has a default, and every default is occasionally a disaster. Dropping incomplete rows is the R default and it can quietly delete a season. Replacing missing values with the mean is the commonest imputation and it manufactures data that was never observed. Removing outliers is standard practice and it is how genuine extreme events get erased from the record. None of these decisions is technical. Each one requires you to know why the value is missing, or why the number is strange. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea ### Three kinds of missing The distinction matters because only one of them is harmless. **Missing completely at random.** The chance of a value being absent has nothing to do with anything — a technician dropped a tube. Rare in practice. Dropping these rows costs you precision and nothing else. **Missing at random** (a badly named category). The chance depends on things you *did* observe: chlorophyll is missing more often in winter, and you recorded the season. Dropping the rows biases your sample; imputation using the observed variables can repair much of it. **Missing not at random.** The chance depends on the missing value itself. A sensor that fails in rough weather, and rough weather is when the interesting mixing happens. A net that fails to retain the smallest individuals. Nothing in the data can fix this, and no imputation method will tell you that you have it. You have to know your instrument. Our chlorophyll gap is the middle case: 19% missing in winter, 1% in autumn, with season recorded. But ask *why* the winter values are absent. If it is cloud cover blocking an ocean-colour sensor, then cloudy days are missing — and cloud affects light, which affects chlorophyll. Framed that way, the same gap is closer to the third kind. ### Outliers come in three kinds too **Impossible values.** A depth of 1581 m on a 200 m shelf. A salinity of $-999$. These are errors. Correct them if you can reconstruct the truth, otherwise mark them missing. **Genuine extremes.** A single haul with 400 individuals during a spawning aggregation. This is the most valuable observation in your dataset, and "outlier removal" deletes it. Extreme is not the same as wrong. **Plausible errors.** The two depths that are ten times too deep but land inside the normal range. Undetectable, and they stay in your data. ::: {.callout-warning} "More than three standard deviations from the mean" is not a definition of an error. It is a definition of rare, and in ecological count data rare values are usually the real ones. Remove a value because you can say what is wrong with it, not because it is far from the middle. ::: ### Measurement error The vessel offset found on the [previous page](exploratory-analysis.qmd) is not a missing value or an outlier. It is a systematic bias in an instrument, and it affects every row that vessel collected. Three options, in descending order of preference: correct it against a calibration standard; include `vessel` as a feature so the model can absorb the offset; or drop salinity, which here costs nothing since salinity has no real effect. ### Class imbalance When one class is rare — the 5% rare species — two things follow. Accuracy becomes meaningless, as [section 1 showed](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd). And the fitting procedure itself is pulled towards the common class, because getting the common class right is where the easy gains are. Remedies exist: down-sampling the common class, up-sampling the rare one, synthetic methods such as SMOTE, or class weights. All are available through the `themis` package as recipe steps, and all come with the same condition: ::: {.callout-important} Resampling for imbalance is applied to the **training data only**, never to the data you evaluate on. Balancing your test set means measuring performance on a population that does not exist. In `recipes` this is handled for you — `themis` steps are skipped when the recipe is applied to new data — but only if you use them inside a recipe rather than balancing the table by hand beforehand. ::: ## Worked example ### Sentinels first ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean <- raw |> distinct() |> mutate( salinity_psu = na_if(salinity_psu, -999), temperature_c = na_if(temperature_c, -999) ) clean |> summarise(across(c(temperature_c, salinity_psu, chlorophyll_mg_m3), list(missing = \(x) sum(is.na(x)), mean = \(x) round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 2)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| temperature_c_missing| temperature_c_mean| salinity_psu_missing| salinity_psu_mean| chlorophyll_mg_m3_missing| chlorophyll_mg_m3_mean| |---------------------:|------------------:|--------------------:|-----------------:|-------------------------:|----------------------:| | 8| 8.63| 24| 33.92| 51| 1.43|
::: ::: Salinity's mean moves from 2.24 to 33.9. Nothing was fixed in the data — the `-999`s are still missing values — but they are now *honestly* missing, and every summary downstream stops lying. ### Categories ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean <- clean |> mutate(substrate = str_to_lower(str_trim(substrate)), substrate = fct_collapse(substrate, sand = c("sand", "sandy"), mud = c("mud", "muddy"), gravel = "gravel", rock = c("rock", "rocky"))) count(clean, substrate) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|substrate | n| |:---------|---:| |gravel | 139| |mud | 303| |rock | 55| |sand | 303|
::: ::: Note the judgement hidden in that block. Is `sandy` the same category as `sand`, or was one observer distinguishing "sand" from "sandy mud"? We have merged them. On a real survey this is a question for whoever recorded it, and the honest version of this code comes with an answer, not an assumption. ### Impossible depths ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean |> filter(depth_m > 250) |> select(station_id, depth_m) |> arrange(desc(depth_m)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station_id | depth_m| |:----------|-------:| |ST0054 | 1581| |ST0584 | 1463| |ST0284 | 1392| |ST0145 | 1335| |ST0677 | 1174| |ST0129 | 1052| |ST0202 | 1051| |ST0344 | 808| |ST0167 | 629| |ST0655 | 283|
::: ::: Ten stations, all suspiciously close to ten times a plausible shelf depth. Dividing by ten puts each one back into the range where its temperature makes sense, which is evidence rather than convenience — a station recorded at 1581 m with 6 °C water is impossible on this shelf, while the same station at 158 m is ordinary. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean <- clean |> mutate(depth_m = if_else(depth_m > 250, depth_m / 10, depth_m)) range(clean$depth_m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 5.0 194.6 ``` ::: ::: Two of the twelve decimal errors are still in there, at 125 m and 166 m, and no inspection will find them. That is the normal state of a cleaned dataset. ### What complete-case deletion would cost The default in most modelling functions is to silently drop any row with a missing value. Here is the bill. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} comparison <- bind_rows( clean |> count(season) |> mutate(dataset = "All rows"), clean |> drop_na() |> count(season) |> mutate(dataset = "Complete cases only") ) ggplot(comparison, aes(season, n, fill = dataset)) + geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.68) + geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Stations", fill = NULL, title = "Where the deleted rows come from") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Season composition of the survey before and after dropping every row with a missing value. Winter loses about a fifth of its stations, and the dataset quietly becomes less wintry than the survey that produced it.](missing-values-and-outliers_files/figure-html/fig-deletion-1.png){#fig-deletion fig-alt='Grouped bar chart comparing the number of stations per season before and after complete-case deletion. Autumn, spring and summer barely change, while winter drops visibly from just over 200 stations to around 165.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( rows_before = nrow(clean), rows_after = nrow(drop_na(clean)), lost = nrow(clean) - nrow(drop_na(clean)), winter_lost_pct = round(100 * (1 - sum(drop_na(clean)$season == "winter") / sum(clean$season == "winter")), 1) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| rows_before| rows_after| lost| winter_lost_pct| |-----------:|----------:|----:|---------------:| | 800| 720| 80| 20.1|
::: ::: About 10% of rows overall — and a fifth of winter. If your question involves winter conditions, the default has just removed a fifth of your evidence about them, without a warning. ## What the results mean The alternative is imputation: predict the missing chlorophyll values from the variables you do have. `recipes` offers several steps — `step_impute_median()`, `step_impute_knn()`, `step_impute_bag()` — and the [next page](scaling-and-encoding.qmd) puts them into a recipe properly. Two conditions on imputation, both routinely broken: **It must happen inside the resampling, not before.** Imputing with the median of the whole dataset uses test-set values to fill training-set gaps. That is leakage, it is easy to do by accident, and it is [the last page of this section](information-leakage.qmd). **An imputed value is not an observation.** It is a prediction with uncertainty, and treating it as data understates how little you know. Adding a `was_missing` indicator column costs one feature and lets the model — and you — see where the gaps were. For this dataset, the defensible chain is: sentinels to `NA`; categories standardised; impossible depths corrected with a stated justification; chlorophyll imputed inside the resampling with a missingness indicator; the vessel offset either corrected or absorbed by including `vessel` as a feature. Not one of those steps is a default. ## Where this breaks down **Imputation cannot recover information that was never there.** With 19% of winter chlorophyll missing, winter estimates will be weaker than summer ones whatever you do. The honest response is to say so, not to impute until the table looks full. **Correcting outliers can manufacture the pattern you are looking for.** We divided ten depths by ten because the result fitted the rest of the survey. That reasoning is sound and it is also how confirmation bias operates. State the rule, apply it uniformly, and report how many rows it touched. **Balancing classes changes what the model is estimating.** Down-sampling gives a model trained on a 50/50 world when yours is 5/95, so its predicted probabilities no longer mean what they say. [Section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) covers calibration. **Cleaning is a scientific record, not a chore.** Every decision here changes the results and should appear in the methods. "Data were cleaned in R" is not a method. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Ask *why* a value is missing. Missing-in-winter and missing-at-random need different responses, and missing-because-of-the-value cannot be fixed at all. - Complete-case deletion is the silent default. Here it removes about a fifth of winter. - Impossible, extreme and plausible-but-wrong are three different kinds of outlier. Only the first is safely removed; the second is often your most valuable data. - Systematic instrument bias is not an outlier. Correct it, or let the model see which instrument took each reading. - Balance classes on the training data only, and expect predicted probabilities to shift when you do. - Impute inside the resampling, never before it, and keep a record of where the gaps were. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Compare `step_impute_median()` with `step_impute_knn()` on chlorophyll. How different are the imputed winter values, and which set looks more like real winter chlorophyll? 2. Suppose the missing chlorophyll is caused by cloud, and cloud reduces light and hence chlorophyll. Which of the three kinds of missingness is that, and does any imputation method fix it?
